fullContext:
Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Hey, everyone, and welcome back to the Information, uh, Bottleneck Podcast. And today we have Zhuang Liu. He's a assistant professor, uh, at Princeton. Hi, Zhuang. Nice to have you.

Zhuang Liu: Hi, Ravid. Mm. Hi, Alan. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And as always, we have Alan. Hey, Alan.

Allen Roush: It's good to see you again, Ravid. Nice to meet you, Zhuang. And, uh, yeah, you should go take a look at his Google Scholar. He has a lot of really cool papers.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Yeah, so we'll talk about some of these papers, uh, today. And in general, we are going to talk about what are the important components, uh, in today AIs. Okay? So you have so, Zhuang, you have so many works. Uh, I think we can start with some understanding of what do you think are the important component. So, uh, a few years ago, you had a paper about, uh, a conv, a convnet for the 2020s, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, that, you know what? Maybe you'll tell us about what is the, the paper about, and then we can start to, to start to decompose the-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... the components for current, uh, AI systems.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. So the paper, we, we were working on this paper in twen- 2021, and back then, transformers has just entered the computer vision's, world, computer vision research space, through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

They're still playing around with architectures, like how do you, how do you change residual connections? How do you, connect different layers? these kind of stuff. And, and I respect that work a lot. In fact, part of the reason that architecture research is less active in academia right now is that, we couldn't really afford to, afford the compute to demonstrate these effects in, in, convincing scale. So that's a, a sad part, but I still try to play around with it myself using our, resources at, at, university. actually, with the help of Cloud Code, I can now, go back to coding to, to play around in the first hand myself. So this is very fun research, but in, I do think in, from a practical stand, point of view, what data we learn, what data we train the model on matters more than, the architecture choice.

As long as the interface, the input/output interface stays the same, architecture, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The, the very basic function of, of neural networks or deep learning. And how we parameterize it, no matter, as long as you get like a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or, or other like, reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward, layers at the right places, you'll be at the f- very close or at the frontier, curve of this, performance, versus efficiency, balance. And, then I was, I, I would tend to think that what, what matters more in terms of practical usage, in terms of bringing the product to more and more people to be more effective in their daily usage.

I do think other, other aspects like what data has this model been trained on, how it can handle context and memory is what, what matters more. So in terms of context and memory, yes, there are-- there do exist architectural work that, address that. So I think that is kind of the more immediate problems we, we need to address in, in making AI like up another level. Yeah.

Allen Roush: In a ConvNet for the 2020s, uh, first of all, you know, maybe just give your summary of that paper, but, but then my, my question is, um, you know, as I read it, uh, it looks like you, you gr-- and also correct me if this, uh, uh, my understanding is wrong, but my understanding is you gradually modernize ResNet towards a Swin-like design and end up-

Zhuang Liu: Right

Allen Roush: ... with a ConvNet that competes strongly with transformers. Um, which single ablation did you, like in that paper, most changed your own mind about where the supposed transformer advantage was really coming from?

Zhuang Liu: what ablation? I think it's every ablation. If you, if you look at the graph, nothing single-handedly, transformed, like brought, brought up the performance by large margin. Like some of them are more useful than others, but, it's not really that one change changed everything. maybe the, I, I guess the use of activation and norm-- redu-reduction of normalization layers is one thing that, kind of intrigued me and, has a noticeable performance change. but it was really everything together. So these seemingly small components, when we compound them together, they can, they can really cause large differences that would normally attribute to, some, some substantial change, like changing convolution to a self-attention or in, into, modernized, say, more modern mechanisms like linear attention, right?

So, so I think the, the big lesson here is, these small details when combined together matters much more than the sim- seemingly core components of the networks. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think it's-- because for me, it looks that like we have, like we are trying a lot of things. Some of these things are working, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then we get better models.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then like in retrospective, like we can, we can start like to understand like exactly what the component that are actually matter, right? Like we can-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... try to, oh, so now let's change ConvNet and, and make it look, looks more as a, as a transformer, for example, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, do you agree with that? Do you think that like this is something that we actually need, need this breakthrough, and then we can trace back and, uh, understand the, the details and try to match other methods? Or do you think like we just need to try again and again, and, uh, we don't need the very specific, uh, directions?

I see. Got it. Yeah, I think transformer absolutely is a blessing to the, to the community and also the vision transformers, the, the adoption of transformers in computer vision. I don't debate that. That's, that's hard to debate. it's, it's absolutely a breakthrough, a very important breakthrough. perh- perhaps the, the biggest breakthrough in, in that, years. and, so our study was more focusing on like computer vision only domains. But another benefit of vision transformers is that they, they allow the unification of, of text and image representations, right? it's, it's then the use of transformer is very important for later developments like, LLaVA, like this multimodal framework where you have text enc-- vision encoders encode the vision into tokens, and then just treat tokens, get them together to be fed into a, a downstream LLMs.

It's a basic framework of a lot of multimodal models right now. So I think, the adoption of transformers in vision is v- a big stamp, big step for unification of multimodal data. This is, back to the, our study. Investigation of details, I, I would say it's more of a lesson. It's l- not, I think it changed my understanding more than, more than like... I'm, I'm more proud of this work because it changes my own understanding and some other, a lot of other people's understanding rather than like we now can go really, like you can still stay with ConvNets. I, I-- people can still do that. The ConvNets has its own benefits as well, especially when, restricted to computer vision only.

It's, it's convenient to deploy. It's, kind of easier to understand, especially it, may also have, better support for higher resolution long con-- long, long sequences because the operation is local. I, I, I think they just excel at different places. and this, this study-... transformation of details is a, a, is more kind of a lesson for me rather than like, we need to figure out each component, how, how much they contributes to, to performance, difference. Yeah.

astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think that's a very good point. I, I do agree that we need these new directions. Our work was, in some sense, looking back after vision transformers became successful, right? We had this very strong reference, and then we could ask, okay, which parts of this design are actually responsible for the improvement? Without that reference, it's much harder to know what you should change in a convnet.

So I wouldn't interpret our result as saying that we don't need breakthroughs, or we should just keep trying small changes forever. Even if you eventually reach similar performance, a new architecture can give you a new perspective on the design space. It makes you reconsider choices that you might have taken for granted. And those lessons can sometimes transfer back to the older architectures. I think that's a very useful outcome itself.

But, but at the same time, when a new model works better, we shouldn't immediately attribute everything to its most distinctive component. That's where this retrospective study becomes important. You need the exploration, somebody trying a different direction, and then you also need the careful experiments to understand what actually mattered. So I think these two kinds of work support each other. The new direction helps us discover things, and the controlled study helps us understand what we discovered.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think it’s a little bit of both. In our case, the vision transformer—and especially Swin—gave us a very useful reference point. It showed that this particular combination of design choices could work extremely well, and then we could go back and ask: which parts are really due to self-attention, and which parts are simply better training recipes or better architectural details? Without that breakthrough, the search space is so large that it would be difficult to know where to look.

But I also wouldn’t say that we can just copy the new model backward and then fully understand it. A lot of the individual changes are small, and their effects depend on the other choices around them. So you still need careful experiments and, honestly, quite a lot of trial and error. The important thing is that the trial and error should be organized around a hypothesis. You control the components, do the ablations, and see whether the story survives.

So breakthroughs are valuable partly because they give us a new direction and a new point on the frontier. Then this kind of retrospective decomposition tells us what was actually essential and what was incidental. And sometimes the conclusion is that the headline explanation—like, “attention is fundamentally better than convolution”—was too simple. Yeah.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I think it's, it's honestly both, and they're kind of coupled. so to be, to be very honest about our own work, ConvNeXt would not exist without vision transformers. Like, we, we did not come up with those design choices out of, out of thin air. The, the patchify stem, the, the large kernel, the inverted bottleneck, the, the fewer norm layers, fewer activations, a lot of that was, was basically reading off what the transformer people had, had already found and asking, okay, is this actually about self-attention, or is this just, a good design that we can also have? So in that sense, yes, you, you need someone to make the bold jump first, because the bold jump is what, what resets the search space and tells the community, there's a whole region over here that nobody has looked at.

but then, I, I would say most of the actual, the actual gains come from the, the second phase, the, the filling in. and, and that phase is much less glamorous, and it's also much harder to get credit for. because when you, when you trace back afterwards, the, the story that gets told is, "transformers beat convnets," right? And, and the real story is more like, the transformer paper came with, thirty, forty small decisions attached to it, and, and it took the community two, three years to figure out which of those were load-bearing.

so I, I don't think it's, you, you need the specific direction or you need the random search. it's more that the, the breakthrough gives you a, a new prior over where to search, and then the, the trying again and again is what, what actually converts that prior into, into performance. and, and the sad thing, going back to what I said earlier, is that the second phase is the part that, that academia used to be able to do, and, and now it's getting harder because of compute. So we're, we're increasingly in a situation where the jumps happen somewhere and, and nobody has the resources to go back and, and carefully figure out what actually mattered. Yeah.

grok.text:
I think it's, it's a mix of both, honestly. I, I wouldn't say we only need one or the other.

So, so if you look at that ConvNet paper, right, we, we actually needed the vision transformer moment. Like, without that, without people showing that this other family of models can, can get to a much stronger point, we wouldn't even have known that there is this, this extra room sitting there for convnets. The, the transformer work was kind of an existence proof. It told us, okay, the, the frontier can be here. And then we could go back and ask, is this because of self-attention, or is this because of a bunch of other design choices that came along with it? And, and it turned out to be more of the second.

So I do think these, these kind of breakthroughs, or, or at least these strong empirical results, they are very useful as a, as a signal. They, they tell you where the Pareto frontier might be, and then you can try to reverse-engineer, decompose, match, like you said. That's, that's a very productive loop.

But I also don't think we should sit there and wait for the next big conceptual jump, and only then start tracing back. A lot of the, the actual progress is, is this more boring process of, of trying things, compounding small details, seeing what sticks. And, and sometimes you don't even fully understand why it works until much later. That's, that's okay. I, I think that's how a lot of architecture work actually happens.

The, the danger is if we, if we only chase the, the story of one core idea, like convolution versus attention, and we ignore the, the many small components around it. Then we, we mis-attribute where the gain is coming from. And, and then we also, we also underinvest in just exploring the design space carefully.

So, so for me, the, the useful research mode is: when there is a breakthrough, treat it as a, a new reference point, not as a, not as proof that one mechanism is inherently superior. Then go back, modernize the other methods, see if they catch up. And in parallel, keep trying, keep iterating, especially on the parts that actually seem to matter more now, like data, like context, like memory. You don't always need a very specific grand direction. You, you need a good question, enough compute to, to make the comparison convincing, and then the patience to, to look at the details. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think that's a very good point, and I largely agree with that. In deep learning, research often progresses in this kind of cycle. When someone introduces a breakthrough or a radically new paradigm—like Vision Transformers—they usually don't just change one single component. They bring along a whole package: a new training recipe, different optimizers, modern data augmentation, and new architectural heuristics. 

And because everything is changed at once and it achieves state-of-the-art results, it breaks us out of the local optima we were stuck in. People had been tuning ConvNets with the same standard recipe from 2015 for years, and we kind of hit a plateau because nobody was questioning those default settings anymore. So you need that kind of "shock" or breakthrough to expand the horizon and show what is possible.

But then, once that happens, I think the retrospective work is equally important. That's the scientific part—to trace back, disentangle the factors, and really understand: what was actually driving the performance gain? Is it truly the core mechanism like self-attention, or is it all the modern training techniques and macro design choices surrounding it? 

So I think both are necessary. Without those bold breakthroughs, we probably wouldn't even think to explore those directions or change our established habits. But without the careful retrospective analysis, we risk drawing the wrong conclusions about why things work.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I think that's a, a really good question. So if I, if I reflect on our own work, it was very much the, the first mode, right? The breakthrough had already happened, we had vision transformers, we had Swin transformers, and they were, they were clearly ahead of, of the conventional convnets at that time. And what we did was, was really tracing back, like, decomposing which of those components actually brought the gains. So I think having the, the breakthrough there as a target was, was extremely useful, because it gives you a, a reference point. You know what level of performance is, is achievable, and then you can study, one design choice at a time, how to close the gap.

But, but I also don't think that's the whole story, because if you ask where did the breakthrough itself come from, transformers, attention, self-attention, these were also developed through many years of, of people trying different things. And when vision transformer first came out, a lot of people, including, including myself, were, were somewhat skeptical, right? So somebody had to, to just try it and make it work, before there was anything to, to trace back from. So I, I would say these two modes are, are kind of complementary, and they, they feed into each other. A breakthrough opens up a new region of the design space, and then the careful, retrospective study tells you which parts actually matter. And that understanding, in turn, kind of seeds the next, next breakthrough.

And I think one thing that, that has changed is the, the scale you need to, to convincingly verify a new idea. In the past, maybe you could demonstrate, a breakthrough on a relatively modest setup, like on small-scale tasks. But today, to convince people that your new architecture or, or your new recipe is really better, you almost have to show it at, at very large scale, right? So the, the trying-again-and-again part has become much more expensive, especially for, for academia. And that's, that's partly why a lot of the exploratory work has moved to, to industry labs, and the rest of us are doing more of, of the understanding and, and distilling part. But, but I do think both are, are essential to, to how the field, moves forward. Yeah.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a, that's a very good question. I, I think it's kind of both, actually. so, so I don't think we can just randomly try things without any direction. Like the search space is, is too large, right? You need some, some hypothesis, some, kind of prior about what might work. but where does the prior come from? in, in my experience it usually comes from, from these breakthroughs, like somebody demonstrates something new, like vision transformers, and then everybody, everybody notices, oh, this model does things differently from what we were doing before, in, in many small ways. And then that gives you a, a very concrete direction to, to explore.

So in that sense, yes, I, I do think the breakthrough is, is kind of necessary, at least it's, it's very helpful, because it, it gives you a new reference point. And then the, the retrospective work, like what we did in ConvNeXt, is, is actually very important too, because otherwise people will attribute the gain to the wrong thing, right? Like back then, everyone was saying, oh, it's, it's self-attention, self-attention is the magic. and if we didn't do this kind of controlled study, that, that belief would just, kind of stay in the community and, and guide the next, next several years of research in a, in a maybe wrong direction. so I, I see these two as, as complementary. The, the breakthrough kind of, expands the space, and the, the careful, controlled study kind of, cleans it up and tells you what really, what really mattered.

but I would also say, if you look at the breakthroughs themselves, like the transformer itself, they, they were also, kind of, a combination of many, many small things that were tried again and again, right? Like the attention mechanism existed before, residual connections existed before, layer norm existed before. it's, it's, the people who put them together at the right time with the right, right scale. So even the, the breakthrough is, is not really one, one single idea from nowhere. it, it's more like a, like an accumulation, and then at some point it, it, it crosses some threshold and, and everyone notices. so, so from that perspective, the, the "try again and again" part, and the, the "breakthrough" part, they're, they're actually the same process, just, just viewed at different, different time scales. yeah.

And, and I think one, one nice thing for, for academia is that the second part, the, the tracing back, is, is something we can still afford to do. Like we, we can't train the frontier model, but we can, we can take what's out there and ask, okay, which of these ten design choices actually matter, and, and that, that knowledge is, I think, very, very valuable to the, the whole community. Yeah.
